angle: How a 1941 walk in the Swiss Alps with a burr-covered dog led George de Mestral to spend over a decade turning a plant's hook-and-loop trick into Velcro
mustEstablish: Who George de Mestral was: Swiss electrical engineer, born 1907, with a curious/inventive streak before this story
Where the walk happened: the Alps near his home in Switzerland (sometimes specified as near Lake Geneva/the Jura), and roughly when (commonly dated 1941)
What a burr actually is: the hooked seed-pod of plants like burdock (Arctium), evolved to snag fur/clothing for seed dispersal
What de Mestral saw under the microscope: tiny hooks on the burr that caught on the loops of fabric/fur
That turning this observation into a usable product took many years (roughly 1941 to 1955), including failures finding the right material and manufacturing method
That nylon and weaving/heat-treating techniques were key to making durable hooks and loops industrially
The origin of the name Velcro (velours + crochet, French for velvet and hook)
When the patent was filed/granted and when the product reached market
What else Velcro was used for early on / why it mattered (clothing, later NASA use) to give the discovery stakes
